Dishes made with tomato.Gazpacho: This chilled Andalusian soup predates tomatoes in Spain; early versions were bread, garlic and oil, and tomatoes only joined after the 1500s.
Dishes made with tomato.Bruschetta: The name comes from Italian for roasting over coals. Traditionally it is just grilled garlic bread with oil, and the tomato topping is a later favorite.
Dishes made with tomato.Marinara: Despite sounding like 'of the sea', classic marinara has no seafood. It is a quick tomato, garlic and herb sauce said to be made by sailors.
Dishes made with tomato.Shakshuka: Eggs poached in spiced tomato and pepper sauce, beloved from Tunisia to Israel. Its name is often traced to an Arabic word for 'mixture'.
Dishes made with tomato.Caprese: This salad of tomato, mozzarella and basil mirrors the Italian flag's colors. It is named for the island of Capri.
Dishes made with tomato.Ketchup: Ketchup began as a fermented fish sauce from Southeast Asia. Tomatoes did not become its main ingredient until the early 1800s.
Dishes made with tomato.Pico de gallo: Mexican fresh salsa of chopped tomato, onion, chili and cilantro. Its name means 'rooster's beak', and nobody agrees why.
Dishes made with tomato.Margherita pizza: Legend says a Naples pizzaiolo made it in 1889 for Queen Margherita, using tomato, mozzarella and basil to echo Italy's flag.
Dishes made with tomato.Bloody Mary: Tomato juice is the base of this brunch cocktail, usually spiked with vodka. Many claim it as a hangover cure, though evidence is thin.
Dishes made with tomato.Ratatouille: This Provençal stew of tomato, eggplant, zucchini and peppers began as a humble peasant dish, and a 2007 Pixar film made it famous worldwide.
Dishes made with tomato.Panzanella: A Tuscan salad that rescues stale bread by soaking it with ripe tomatoes, cucumber, onion and oil. It dates back centuries.
Dishes made with tomato.Bolognese: Real ragù alla bolognese is mostly meat, slow-cooked with only a little tomato, and in Bologna it is served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti.
Dishes made with tomato.Salsa roja: Spanish for 'red sauce', this Mexican table staple is cooked or blended from tomatoes and chilies. Every household has its own version.
Dishes made with tomato.Pesto: This one skips tomato entirely. Genoese pesto is crushed basil, pine nuts, garlic, cheese and oil, and its name comes from 'to pound'.
Dishes made with tomato.Carbonara: Roman carbonara gets its creaminess from egg, pecorino and guanciale. A tomato in it would start a fight in Italy.
Dishes made with tomato.Alfredo: Alfredo is butter, Parmesan and pasta water, with no tomato. It was created in Rome around 1914 by restaurateur Alfredo di Lelio.
Dishes made with tomato.Hummus: Chickpeas, tahini, lemon and garlic, with no tomato. The Arabic word hummus simply means 'chickpeas'.
Dishes made with tomato.Tzatziki: This Greek dip is strained yogurt, cucumber and garlic. It is white and tomato-free, and closely related to Turkish cacik.
Dishes made with tomato.Baba ganoush: Smoky roasted eggplant blended with tahini and lemon. Eggplant is a tomato's cousin in the nightshade family, yet the dish has no tomato.
Dishes made with tomato.Cacio e pepe: Just pecorino cheese, black pepper and pasta water. The Roman classic needs no tomato, and its creamy sauce is famously tricky to emulsify.
Dishes made with tomato.Béchamel: One of French cuisine's mother sauces, made from milk thickened with a butter and flour roux. It is white, not red.
Dishes made with tomato.Hollandaise: An emulsion of egg yolk and butter with lemon, essential to eggs Benedict. It is another French mother sauce, with no tomato.
Dishes made with tomato.Aioli: A garlic and olive oil emulsion from the Mediterranean. Traditional aioli has no egg, and the name is Provençal for 'garlic and oil'.
Dishes made with tomato.Coleslaw: Shredded cabbage in a creamy dressing. The name comes from Dutch 'koolsla', meaning cabbage salad, not from anything cool.

Animals native to Australia.Kangaroo: Australia has more kangaroos than people. A large red kangaroo can cover about 8 metres in a single bound.
Animals native to Australia.Koala: Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most animals. They also have fingerprints very similar to humans'.
Animals native to Australia.Wombat: A burrowing marsupial from Australia and Tasmania. It makes cube-shaped droppings, which it uses to mark territory.
Animals native to Australia.Platypus: Australia's egg-laying mammal. When European scientists first saw a specimen, some suspected a hoax made of several animals.
Animals native to Australia.Echidna: A spiny, egg-laying mammal found in Australia and New Guinea. It has a long snout and a sticky tongue for catching ants.
Animals native to Australia.Emu: The second-tallest living bird, only the ostrich being taller. Australia once fought the Great Emu War in 1932 and lost.
Animals native to Australia.Kookaburra: The laughing kookaburra is the largest kingfisher. Its famous laughter marks its territory at dawn and dusk.
Animals native to Australia.Quokka: A small wallaby-like marsupial found mostly on Rottnest Island off Western Australia, and known for its smiley face.
Animals native to Australia.Tasmanian devil: A marsupial scavenger named for its eerie screeches. Once found across Australia, it survives in the wild only in Tasmania.
Animals native to Australia.Cassowary: A large flightless bird of northern Queensland and New Guinea, with a helmet-like casque on its head. It is dangerous when cornered.
Animals native to Australia.Frilled lizard: When threatened, it flares out a big neck frill and may rise to run on two legs. It lives in northern Australia and New Guinea.
Animals native to Australia.Taipan: Australia's inland taipan is regarded as having the most toxic venom of any snake, though it's shy and rarely bites people.
Animals native to Australia.Lyrebird: A ground-dwelling bird whose tail looks like a lyre. Males are remarkable mimics, even copying camera shutters and chainsaws.
Animals native to Australia.Kiwi: A trap: the kiwi is a symbol of New Zealand, not Australia. It is a flightless bird with nostrils at the tip of its bill.
Animals native to Australia.Lemur: Found naturally only in Madagascar, nowhere near Australia. Madagascar and Australia both have unusual animals, so people mix them up.
Animals native to Australia.Panda: The giant panda is native to the mountains of central China. It is not found anywhere in Australia.
Animals native to Australia.Sloth: A Central and South American animal. It is famous for hanging upside down, and it isn't native to Australia.
Animals native to Australia.Ostrich: A flightless African bird. Australia's similar big bird is the emu, but the ostrich is native to Africa.
Animals native to Australia.Rabbit: A common sight in Australia but not native. Rabbits were introduced in the 1800s and became a huge pest.
Animals native to Australia.Camel: Australia has a large wild camel population, but camels were imported in the 1800s. They aren't native.
Animals native to Australia.Red fox: Introduced to Australia in the 1800s for hunting. The fox has devastated many native small mammals.
Animals native to Australia.Llama: A South American animal from the Andes, not native to Australia, though farmed there in small numbers.
Animals native to Australia.Raccoon: A North American mammal, with a mask-like face. It isn't native to Australia.
Animals native to Australia.Meerkat: A small mongoose from southern Africa. It is not native to Australia, despite living in dry, open country.

Former names of cities.Bombay: Renamed Mumbai in 1995 after the local goddess Mumbadevi. The old name came from Portuguese roots and was used by the British for centuries.
Former names of cities.Peking: This old spelling comes from a Western romanization of the Chinese name. It survives in Peking duck and Peking University, even though the city is Beijing.
Former names of cities.Constantinople: Named for Emperor Constantine, it was the Byzantine capital for over a thousand years until the Ottomans took it in 1453. Istanbul became the official name in 1930.
Former names of cities.Saigon: The southern Vietnamese city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976 after the war ended. Many locals still call it Saigon, especially its central district.
Former names of cities.Leningrad: Founded as Saint Petersburg, it became Petrograd, then Leningrad after Lenin died in 1924. It endured a near 900-day siege in World War II, then reverted in 1991.
Former names of cities.Madras: Renamed Chennai in 1996. The old name lives on in the cotton fabric madras, whose bright plaids were once woven near the city and exported worldwide.
Former names of cities.Calcutta: Renamed Kolkata in 2001 to match the Bengali pronunciation. It was the capital of British India until 1911, when the seat moved to Delhi.
Former names of cities.New Amsterdam: The Dutch settlement on the tip of Manhattan was seized by the English in 1664 and renamed for the Duke of York. It became New York.
Former names of cities.Edo: Edo was the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns and grew into one of the world's biggest cities by 1700. It was renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital, in 1868.
Former names of cities.Batavia: The Dutch East India Company named its Asian headquarters after an ancient tribe, the Batavi. It became Jakarta after Indonesia gained independence.
Former names of cities.Byzantium: This small Greek colony on the Bosphorus predates Constantine's rebuilding of it. Its name gave us the term Byzantine Empire, though its people called themselves Romans.
Former names of cities.Rangoon: Myanmar's largest city was called Rangoon under British rule. Its present name, Yangon, was adopted in 1989, but the capital is now Naypyidaw.
Former names of cities.Mumbai: The city's current name since 1995, so it is not a former one. It sits on seven islands that were joined into one landmass by land reclamation.
Former names of cities.Beijing: The current name of China's capital, meaning northern capital. It's not a former name, though it was often spelled Peking in the West.
Former names of cities.Istanbul: Today's name is not a former one. It is the only major city spanning two continents, Europe and Asia, split by the Bosphorus strait.
Former names of cities.Kolkata: The present-day name, not a former one. Its Howrah Bridge is among the busiest cantilever bridges on Earth, and it was once home to a famous tramway.
Former names of cities.Jakarta: This is the current name, not a past one. Heavy groundwater pumping makes parts of it sink so fast that Indonesia is building a new capital, Nusantara.
Former names of cities.Tokyo: The current name, not a former one. The earlier name Edo was swapped out in 1868, and Tokyo's metro area is now the most populous on Earth.
Former names of cities.Yangon: The current name, not a former one. The Shwedagon Pagoda here is said to be covered in tons of gold leaf and topped with thousands of diamonds.
Former names of cities.Chennai: Present-day name, not a former one. Fort St. George here was the first English fortress in India, founded by the East India Company in 1644.
Former names of cities.Manila: The city has kept its name since Spanish times, so it never changed. Its name probably comes from nilad, a mangrove-like plant growing by the Pasig River.
Former names of cities.Lagos: It has kept this name since Portuguese traders arrived in the 1400s. It means lakes in Portuguese, and it was Nigeria's capital until 1991.
Former names of cities.Dubai: Dubai has kept its name, and it grew from a small pearl-diving and trading town into a giant metropolis in a few decades after oil and trade boomed.
Former names of cities.Osaka: This city has long held its name, which means large slope. It was once a rival power center to Edo, and a final battle there in 1615 cemented shogunate rule.

Primates.Human: A primate too: we share about 98 percent of our DNA with chimpanzees. People belong in the great ape family.
Primates.Chimpanzee: Our closest living relatives alongside bonobos. They make and use tools, such as stripped twigs to fish termites from mounds.
Primates.Gorilla: The largest living primate. Despite their fearsome reputation, they are mostly gentle plant-eaters, and each has a unique nose print.
Primates.Orangutan: The name means person of the forest in Malay. These red apes live in Borneo and Sumatra and build a new sleeping nest every night.
Primates.Lemur: Found only in Madagascar, where they evolved in isolation. Ring-tailed lemurs hold stink fights, waving scented tails at rivals.
Primates.Baboon: Large, ground-living monkeys of Africa and Arabia. They live in troops and have dog-like faces.
Primates.Gibbon: A small ape known as the acrobat of the forest, swinging arm over arm. Pairs sing duets that carry for kilometers.
Primates.Bonobo: A close cousin of chimpanzees living only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Their societies are known for being female-led and peaceful.
Primates.Marmoset: A tiny monkey of South America. It's among the smallest primates, and the pygmy marmoset weighs about as much as a few coins.
Primates.Tarsier: A small nocturnal primate with eyes so big each is larger than its brain. It can rotate its head almost 180 degrees.
Primates.Mandrill: The biggest monkey in the world, whose male has a vivid red-and-blue face. It lives in the forests of Central Africa.
Primates.Aye-aye: A strange lemur of Madagascar. It taps on trees and uses a long thin finger to scoop out grubs.
Primates.Capuchin: A clever monkey of Central and South America. Some use stones to crack nuts, and the name comes from monks' hoods.
Primates.Sloth: A trap: not a primate. Sloths belong to the group with anteaters and armadillos, and algae grow in their fur.
Primates.Raccoon: A trap: although the nimble hands look like ours, raccoons are carnivorans, relatives of weasels and bears.
Primates.Koala: A trap: a marsupial that carries its young in a pouch, not a primate, and it sleeps up to 20 hours a day on a eucalyptus diet.
Primates.Red panda: A trap: it's a carnivoran in its own family, not a primate, and it is no relative of the giant panda.
Primates.Meerkat: A trap: a small mongoose relative. It stands upright like a lookout, but it's no primate.
Primates.Squirrel: A trap: a rodent, not a primate, though tree-dwelling and nimble. Its teeth never stop growing.
Primates.Opossum: A trap: a marsupial, not a primate, despite its grasping tail. It famously plays dead when threatened, and it's immune to many snake venoms.
Primates.Flying fox: A trap: a giant fruit bat, so a bat, not a primate. Some have wingspans of about 1.5 meters.
Primates.Mongoose: A trap: a small carnivoran famed for fighting venomous snakes, and in no way related to monkeys or apes.
Primates.Anteater: A trap: a toothless mammal with a long sticky tongue, related to sloths, not primates.
Primates.Hyena: A trap: it looks doglike but is closer to cats and mongooses. Spotted hyenas live in female-led clans.

Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Laws of motion: Three rules from 1687: objects keep moving unless pushed, force equals mass times acceleration, and every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Gravitation: He showed that the force pulling an apple down also holds the Moon in orbit, and he did it with one inverse-square law.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Calculus: He developed it in the 1660s, in parallel with Leibniz, and the two argued bitterly for years over who deserved the credit.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Reflecting telescope: He built the first practical one in 1668, using a curved mirror rather than a lens, avoiding the color fringes of early refractors.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Splitting light: He passed sunlight through a prism and showed that white light is a mix of colors, and a second prism recombines it into white.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Principia: His 1687 masterpiece, Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, is regarded as one of the most important scientific books ever written.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Falling apple: He recalled watching an apple fall in his garden as the spark for his gravity idea. The tale of it hitting his head is a later embellishment.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Binomial theorem: A formula for expanding powers of sums like (a+b) to any power, which he generalized to non-whole-number exponents.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Royal Mint: He ran it as Warden and then Master from 1696, helped reform England's coinage, and sent counterfeiters to the gallows.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Newton's cradle: A desktop toy of swinging steel balls demonstrating momentum is named for him, though he didn't invent it.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Fig Newtons: They are cookies named after a town in Massachusetts, not the scientist, despite the pun.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Relativity: Einstein's theory, not Newton's, and it replaced Newton's gravity with curved spacetime.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Evolution: Darwin's idea of natural selection from 1859, which came long after Newton's death in 1727.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Light bulb: Edison's practical version came in 1879, and Newton died more than a century before that.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Periodic table: Mendeleev's 1869 chart of elements came about 140 years after Newton's death. Newton's alchemy never found it.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876, long after Newton.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Radioactivity: It was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel, over 150 years after Newton's death.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Heliocentrism: It was Copernicus, and Galileo defended it, who put the Sun at the center, not Newton, who simply accepted it.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Pendulum clock: It was Galileo who studied pendulums, and Huygens who made the first pendulum clock in 1656.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Vaccines: Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine in 1796, nearly 70 years after Newton died.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Steam engine: James Watt improved it in the 1760s, after Newton, and Newcomen built the first practical one in 1712.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.DNA: The double helix of DNA was found in 1953, centuries after Newton's death.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Germ theory: Pasteur and Koch developed it in the 1800s, after Newton's time.
Things Isaac Newton is famous for.Big Bang theory: It came from Lemaitre and Hubble's work in the 1920s and 30s, two centuries later.

Constellations that depict animals.Leo: The Lion, whose brightest star Regulus means 'little king'; the Leonid meteors radiate from it.
Constellations that depict animals.Taurus: The Bull holds two famous star clusters, the Pleiades and Hyades, plus the Crab Nebula, a supernova remnant.
Constellations that depict animals.Cancer: The Crab is the faintest zodiac constellation, yet it holds the Beehive Cluster, visible to the naked eye in dark skies.
Constellations that depict animals.Scorpius: The Scorpion has red Antares, 'rival of Mars'; in myth the scorpion killed Orion, so the two sit on opposite sides of the sky.
Constellations that depict animals.Ursa Major: The Great Bear contains the Big Dipper, whose two end stars point the way to Polaris.
Constellations that depict animals.Ursa Minor: The Little Bear's tail tip is Polaris, the North Star, which sits almost exactly above Earth's axis.
Constellations that depict animals.Cygnus: The Swan flies along the Milky Way and is also called the Northern Cross; its brightest star is Deneb.
Constellations that depict animals.Aquila: The Eagle includes Altair, one corner of the Summer Triangle.
Constellations that depict animals.Lepus: The Hare crouches at Orion's feet, as if being hunted by his dogs.
Constellations that depict animals.Pisces: The two fish are tied by a cord, and because of Earth's wobble the Sun now crosses the spring equinox in Pisces.
Constellations that depict animals.Delphinus: The Dolphin is small but neat, and two of its stars, Sualocin and Rotanev, spell the name of an astronomer's assistant backwards.
Constellations that depict animals.Canis Major: The Great Dog holds Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
Constellations that depict animals.Aries: The Ram marked the spring equinox about 2,000 years ago, but Earth's wobble has since moved that point away.
Constellations that depict animals.Orion: A trap: Orion himself is a human hunter, though his companions Canis Major, Lepus and Taurus are animals.
Constellations that depict animals.Cassiopeia: A vain queen in myth, shown as a W-shaped zigzag, and it is a handy way to find the Andromeda Galaxy.
Constellations that depict animals.Andromeda: A chained princess, and her constellation points to the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest big galaxy at about 2.5 million light-years.
Constellations that depict animals.Perseus: A hero who beheaded Medusa; the constellation holds Algol, the 'Demon Star' that dims every 2.9 days.
Constellations that depict animals.Hercules: A mythic hero, and the constellation holds M13, a spectacular globular cluster of hundreds of thousands of stars.
Constellations that depict animals.Gemini: The Twins, Castor and Pollux, are people, and the zodiac sign is also human.
Constellations that depict animals.Virgo: The Maiden is the largest zodiac constellation, home to a huge cluster of galaxies.
Constellations that depict animals.Libra: The Scales are the only zodiac constellation that is an object, not a living thing.
Constellations that depict animals.Aquarius: The Water-Bearer is a human figure pouring water, not an animal.
Constellations that depict animals.Lyra: The Lyre is a musical instrument, and it contains Vega, one of the brightest stars of the summer sky.
Constellations that depict animals.Crux: The Southern Cross is the smallest of the 88 constellations and appears on several national flags.

Released in 1982, Steven Spielberg's alien film became the highest-grossing film ever until Jurassic Park topped it in 1993.
Films first released in the 1980s.Back to the Future: Eric Stoltz was first cast as Marty and filmed for weeks before being replaced by Michael J. Fox.
Films first released in the 1980s.The Breakfast Club: John Hughes's 1985 film about five students in Saturday detention was shot almost entirely in a school library.
Films first released in the 1980s.Top Gun: Tom Cruise flew with Maverick in 1986, and the 2022 sequel earned well over a billion dollars.
Films first released in the 1980s.Ghostbusters: The 1984 comedy's Ecto-1 is a converted 1959 Cadillac, and its slimy ghost Slimer became a cartoon star.
Films first released in the 1980s.Die Hard: Released in 1988, it is often called a Christmas movie, and it was filmed at a Los Angeles tower, Fox Plaza.
Films first released in the 1980s.The Shining: Stanley Kubrick's 1980 horror film was not loved by Stephen King, who wrote the original novel.
Films first released in the 1980s.Gremlins: This 1984 film and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom helped lead to the creation of the PG-13 rating.
Films first released in the 1980s.The Goonies: The 1985 treasure hunt film, from a Steven Spielberg story, features a pirate called One-Eyed Willy.
Films first released in the 1980s.Beetlejuice: Michael Keaton plays the ghoul, but he is on screen for less than 20 minutes in the 1988 film.
Films first released in the 1980s.Rain Man: It won the Best Picture Oscar for 1988, and Dustin Hoffman won Best Actor for playing Raymond.
Films first released in the 1980s.Big: Tom Hanks plays a boy in an adult's body in this 1988 film, the first by a woman director to gross $100 million in the US.
Films first released in the 1980s.Dirty Dancing: Released in 1987, its famous line is 'Nobody puts Baby in a corner', and it was shot largely in Virginia and North Carolina.
Films first released in the 1980s.Jaws: Jaws arrived in 1975, making it a 1970s film, and it is often credited with inventing the summer blockbuster.
Films first released in the 1980s.Grease: Grease came out in 1978, so it belongs to the 1970s, and its soundtrack is one of the best-selling of all time.
Films first released in the 1980s.Rocky: Rocky is from 1976, and the underdog boxing film won Best Picture, but the 1980s only saw its sequels.
Films first released in the 1980s.Star Wars: Star Wars premiered in 1977, a few years before the 1980s, though its sequel The Empire Strikes Back arrived in 1980.
Films first released in the 1980s.Home Alone: Home Alone is from 1990, which makes it a 1990s film, released just after the 1980s ended.
Films first released in the 1980s.Jurassic Park: Jurassic Park is from 1993, and its dinosaurs broke records for CGI, but it is a 1990s film.
Films first released in the 1980s.Titanic: Titanic sailed into theaters in 1997, a 1990s film that earned 11 Oscars and over two billion dollars worldwide.
Films first released in the 1980s.Pretty Woman: Pretty Woman came out in 1990, so it just misses the 1980s, and Julia Roberts became a star with it.
Films first released in the 1980s.Ghost: Ghost is from 1990, a 1990s hit with the pottery wheel scene; Whoopi Goldberg won an Oscar for it.
Films first released in the 1980s.Halloween: Halloween is from 1978, a 1970s film, and John Carpenter made the slasher classic on a tiny budget.
Films first released in the 1980s.Alien: Alien came out in 1979, just before the 1980s began, though its action-packed sequel Aliens arrived in 1986.

Elvis Presley songs.Hound Dog: Big Mama Thornton recorded it first in 1953. Elvis's 1956 version, from a Las Vegas lounge act's arrangement, made it famous.
Elvis Presley songs.Jailhouse Rock: Both the 1957 hit and the film it comes from; the prison dance number in it is among his most famous.
Elvis Presley songs.Suspicious Minds: His last US number one, from 1969, recorded in Memphis, during the comeback after his Hollywood years.
Elvis Presley songs.Love Me Tender: The tune comes from the Civil War-era ballad Aura Lee, and the song names his first film.
Elvis Presley songs.Heartbreak Hotel: Writer Tommy Durden was inspired by a newspaper story about a suicide note; Elvis's 1956 version was his first million-seller.
Elvis Presley songs.All Shook Up: Songwriter Otis Blackwell wrote this 1957 number one, and Elvis got a co-writer credit.
Elvis Presley songs.Return to Sender: A 1962 hit from the film Girls! Girls! Girls!, about a love letter that keeps coming back to the writer.
Elvis Presley songs.Burning Love: Written by Dennis Linde and first recorded by Arthur Alexander, it was Elvis's last top-10 pop hit, in 1972.
Elvis Presley songs.In the Ghetto: A 1969 social commentary written by Mac Davis, and a rare serious song for the King.
Elvis Presley songs.It's Now or Never: The tune is borrowed from the Italian O Sole Mio, adapted in English in 1960 and a worldwide hit.
Elvis Presley songs.Don't Be Cruel: Released as a double-sided single with Hound Dog, it topped the pop, country and R&B charts in 1956.
Elvis Presley songs.Great Balls of Fire: Jerry Lee Lewis's 1957 hit, not Elvis's, though both recorded at Sun Records in Memphis.
Elvis Presley songs.Peggy Sue: Buddy Holly's 1957 song, with its tumbling drums, and not an Elvis recording.
Elvis Presley songs.Ring of Fire: Johnny Cash's 1963 hit, co-written by June Carter, and not Elvis's.
Elvis Presley songs.Sweet Little Sixteen: Chuck Berry's 1958 hit, whose melody the Beach Boys later reused for Surfin' U.S.A.
Elvis Presley songs.La Bamba: Ritchie Valens turned a Mexican folk tune into a 1958 rock hit, and he died the next year at age 17.
Elvis Presley songs.Folsom Prison Blues: Johnny Cash's song, and he recorded a famous live version in front of the prisoners at Folsom.
Elvis Presley songs.Wake Up Little Susie: An Everly Brothers hit from 1957 that was banned by some radio stations, including Boston's.
Elvis Presley songs.Summertime Blues: Eddie Cochran's 1958 teen anthem about having no free time to date, and not an Elvis hit.
Elvis Presley songs.Be-Bop-A-Lula: Gene Vincent's 1956 rockabilly classic, and it was an Elvis-era rival rather than an Elvis song.
Elvis Presley songs.Chantilly Lace: The Big Bopper's 1958 hit, which opens with the phone call 'Hello baby!', and not an Elvis recording.
Elvis Presley songs.Oh Pretty Woman: Roy Orbison's 1964 classic, with its growling intro, and not by Elvis.
Elvis Presley songs.Rave On: Buddy Holly's 1958 hit, a fellow rock pioneer's song and not one from Elvis's catalog.
Elvis Presley songs.Maybellene: Chuck Berry's 1955 debut single, a key early rock and roll record that is not an Elvis one.

Instruments you blow into.Trumpet: Valves added in the early 1800s let trumpets play every note. Before that, players were limited to a few notes of the harmonic series.
Instruments you blow into.Flute: The oldest known instruments are flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory, more than 40,000 years old.
Instruments you blow into.Harmonica: You play it by breathing in and out. Bob Dylan wears his in a neck rack so he can play guitar too.
Instruments you blow into.Recorder: Henry VIII reportedly owned dozens of these, and it later became a classroom staple.
Instruments you blow into.Bagpipes: Air goes into a bag you squeeze, so the sound never stops for a breath.
Instruments you blow into.Didgeridoo: Players use circular breathing, puffing out air while inhaling through the nose, to keep the drone going without a break.
Instruments you blow into.Saxophone: Invented by Adolphe Sax around 1840. It is brass but counts as woodwind thanks to its single reed.
Instruments you blow into.Tuba: Uncoiled, a big tuba's tubing stretches more than five metres.
Instruments you blow into.Ocarina: Made of clay or ceramic. Zelda's Ocarina of Time in 1998 sent its popularity soaring.
Instruments you blow into.Clarinet: A single reed makes it different from the oboe, which uses a double reed.
Instruments you blow into.Oboe: The double reed is tricky and many players make their reeds by hand.
Instruments you blow into.Trombone: The slide has seven positions, and the player's arm decides the pitch.
Instruments you blow into.Melodica: A keyboard you play while blowing through a mouthpiece. Reggae's Augustus Pablo made it his signature sound.
Instruments you blow into.Violin: Bowed or plucked strings, no blowing needed.
Instruments you blow into.Snare drum: A struck drum with metal wires under it. You hit it, not blow it.
Instruments you blow into.Guitar: Strummed or plucked strings. Players use no breath here.
Instruments you blow into.Piano: Hammers strike its strings, so it counts as both a string and a percussion instrument.
Instruments you blow into.Accordion: Air does move over its reeds, but from a bellows squeezed by the arms, not the player's breath. A good trap.
Instruments you blow into.Harp: Plucked strings, with no breath involved.
Instruments you blow into.Xylophone: A percussion instrument made of wooden bars struck with mallets.
Instruments you blow into.Banjo: Strings plucked and strummed, like a guitar.
Instruments you blow into.Cymbal: The Zildjian family has been making them in Istanbul since 1623. Struck, not blown.
Instruments you blow into.Triangle: A bent steel rod struck with a beater, and it is not blown.
Instruments you blow into.Maracas: Gourds filled with seeds, shaken in the hand. Not a wind instrument.

Onomatopoeia.Buzz: Bees do not buzz with their mouths; the sound comes from wings beating roughly 200 times a second.
Onomatopoeia.Bang: This word is also the name of the Big Bang, a term astronomer Fred Hoyle is said to have coined on radio in 1949.
Onomatopoeia.Sizzle: Frying food sizzles because water droplets hit hot oil and flash into steam, popping and spitting as they escape.
Onomatopoeia.Hiss: Geese, cats, snakes and kettles all hiss, so the word imitates a sound shared by very different sources.
Onomatopoeia.Pop: Pop music took its name from 'popular', but the word itself began as imitation of a small, sharp burst of air.
Onomatopoeia.Splash: Comic-book artists draw splashes with starburst shapes, but the word itself copies the sound of water scattering.
Onomatopoeia.Crash: A crash cymbal and a car crash share the word because both make a sudden, noisy collision of hard objects.
Onomatopoeia.Boom: Boom can imitate a deep explosion, but economists also use it for a sudden surge in business or population.
Onomatopoeia.Meow: Adult cats rarely meow at each other; they mostly developed the sound to get attention from humans.
Onomatopoeia.Moo: Cows moo in different tones, and studies suggest mothers and calves recognize one another by their calls.
Onomatopoeia.Tick-tock: Clocks say tick-tock in English, but in many languages they say something different, like 'tic-tac' in French.
Onomatopoeia.Whoosh: Whoosh imitates rushing air, and it is a favorite of comic strips for showing fast movement without any real sound.
Onomatopoeia.Thud: Thud is a dull, heavy sound; it comes from Old English 'thyddan', meaning to strike or thrust.
Onomatopoeia.Quiet: Trap: quiet describes a lack of sound rather than imitating one, so it is a description, not onomatopoeia.
Onomatopoeia.Loud: Trap: loud tells you how a sound feels, but it does not copy any sound the way 'bang' or 'boom' does.
Onomatopoeia.Song: A song is made of sounds, but the word itself is just a label, nothing like the noise it names.
Onomatopoeia.Noise: Noise is a plain label for unwanted sound; it likely comes from Latin 'nausea', not from imitation.
Onomatopoeia.Sound: Sound is a general word for what we hear, and it does not mimic any particular noise.
Onomatopoeia.Music: Music comes from the Greek 'mousike', the art of the Muses, so it has nothing to do with imitating sound.
Onomatopoeia.Volume: Volume comes from the Latin word for a scroll, because books were once rolls, and later meant a size or amount.
Onomatopoeia.Tune: Tune is a variant of 'tone'; it names a melody rather than copying a sound.
Onomatopoeia.Shout: Shout describes how a person speaks loudly, but it does not imitate the sound of a shout.
Onomatopoeia.Melody: Melody comes from Greek words for song and singing, so it describes music rather than echoing a noise.
Onomatopoeia.Silence: Silence is the absence of sound, so by definition it cannot be a word that imitates one.

Parts of a piano.Keys: A modern piano has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black, and the first pianos of around 1700 had only about 49.
Parts of a piano.Hammers: Each key flicks a felt-covered hammer at the strings and then lets it fall away, so the string can keep ringing.
Parts of a piano.Pedals: Most grand pianos have three pedals; the middle one, called sostenuto, holds only the notes already pressed.
Parts of a piano.Strings: A grand piano's strings pull with a combined tension of around 20 tons, which is why its frame is cast iron.
Parts of a piano.Soundboard: The soundboard is a thin wooden panel, often spruce, that amplifies the strings, which would otherwise be nearly silent.
Parts of a piano.Lid: A grand piano's lid can be propped open at different heights, which changes how much sound projects into the room.
Parts of a piano.Dampers: Dampers are felt pads that silence strings when a key is released; lift them all with a pedal and notes blur together.
Parts of a piano.Music stand: On a grand piano the music stand is detachable and sits at the front of the case, above the keys.
Parts of a piano.Frame: The iron frame, or plate, holds enormous string tension, and its invention in the 1800s let pianos grow louder.
Parts of a piano.Fallboard: The fallboard is the hinged cover that closes over the keys, protecting them from dust and from small fingers.
Parts of a piano.Valve: Trap: valves belong to brass instruments, not pianos.
Parts of a piano.Reed: Trap: reeds are for wind instruments like clarinets; a piano's sound comes from hammered strings.
Parts of a piano.Fret: Trap: frets are ridges on guitar necks; a piano's pitches are fixed by each string, not by finger position.
Parts of a piano.Mouthpiece: Trap: you blow into a mouthpiece, but a piano has no airflow.
Parts of a piano.Drumhead: Trap: a drumhead is the struck skin of a drum, though a piano is technically a percussion-and-string hybrid.
Parts of a piano.Bow: Trap: a bow draws across strings on a violin, whereas a piano's strings are struck by hammers.
Parts of a piano.Sound hole: Trap: guitars and violins have sound holes, but a piano's sound comes out the open lid and body.
Parts of a piano.Chanter: Trap: a chanter is the melody pipe of bagpipes, nothing to do with pianos.
Parts of a piano.Spit valve: Trap: spit valves drain moisture from brass instruments; pianos have no such part.
Parts of a piano.Headstock: Trap: headstocks are on guitars, where they hold the tuning pegs; a piano has a pin block instead.
Parts of a piano.Capo: Trap: a capo clamps a guitar's fretboard to raise the pitch; pianos are changed by transposing instead.
Parts of a piano.Bell: Trap: a bell is the flared end of a horn, not a piano part.
Parts of a piano.Slide: Trap: a slide is a trombone part; pianos have no sliding pitch mechanism.
Parts of a piano.Tremolo arm: Trap: the tremolo arm is an electric guitar lever for bending pitch, which a piano cannot do.

Famous violinists.Itzhak Perlman: Born in Tel Aviv, he survived polio as a child and plays seated on stage, and he also played the violin theme of "Schindler's List".
Famous violinists.Yehudi Menuhin: A child prodigy who debuted in New York at 11, he later founded a famed music school in England.
Famous violinists.Niccolò Paganini: His 19th-century virtuosity was so astonishing that rumours said he sold his soul to the devil for it.
Famous violinists.Joshua Bell: In 2007 he played incognito in a Washington subway station, and most commuters hurried past a violin worth millions.
Famous violinists.Anne-Sophie Mutter: The German violinist was discovered by Herbert von Karajan at 13 and plays a Stradivarius.
Famous violinists.Nigel Kennedy: The English violinist's 1989 recording of Vivaldi's "The Four Seasons" became one of the best-selling classical albums ever.
Famous violinists.Hilary Hahn: The American violinist entered the Curtis Institute at 10 and has commissioned new short works called encores from composers.
Famous violinists.Jascha Heifetz: Born in Lithuania in 1901, he is often called the greatest violinist of the 20th century, famed for flawless technique.
Famous violinists.Vanessa-Mae: She released a techno-violin album at 16, and later competed as a skier at the 2014 Winter Olympics for Thailand.
Famous violinists.André Rieu: The Dutch violinist leads the Johann Strauss Orchestra and has filled stadiums with waltzes, and he owns a Stradivarius.
Famous violinists.Nicola Benedetti: The Scottish violinist won BBC Young Musician of the Year at 16 and has championed music education for children.
Famous violinists.Lindsey Stirling: The American violinist rose on YouTube by dancing and playing at once in her videos.
Famous violinists.Yo-Yo Ma: He is a cellist, not a violinist, and he began performing at age 4 or 5, and left his cello in a New York taxi once.
Famous violinists.Jacqueline du Pré: A British cellist whose Elgar concerto recording is legendary, and her career was cut short by multiple sclerosis.
Famous violinists.Lang Lang: The Chinese pianist, who began at 3, performed at the 2008 Beijing Olympics opening ceremony.
Famous violinists.Vladimir Horowitz: The Russian-born pianist was known for thrilling virtuosity, and he reportedly took his own piano on tours.
Famous violinists.Glenn Gould: The Canadian pianist hummed audibly as he played, and he quit live concerts at 31 to record only.
Famous violinists.Arthur Rubinstein: The Polish pianist's career spanned more than 80 years, and he performed into his 90th year.
Famous violinists.Pablo Casals: The Catalan cellist rediscovered Bach's cello suites, which he found in a Barcelona shop at 13.
Famous violinists.James Galway: The Irish flautist, known as "the Man with the Golden Flute", plays an instrument that is not a violin.
Famous violinists.Wynton Marsalis: The trumpeter is the only musician to win Grammys for both jazz and classical in the same year.
Famous violinists.Julian Bream: The English classical guitarist and lutenist helped revive interest in the lute.
Famous violinists.Andrés Segovia: The Spanish guitarist is credited with raising the classical guitar to the concert hall.
Famous violinists.Evelyn Glennie: The Scottish percussionist is profoundly deaf and feels music through her body, often playing barefoot.

Things printed on a shop receipt.Date: Receipts are often required for returns, and the date starts the clock on a warranty or refund window.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Total: The total sits near the bottom, and prices ending in .99 are priced that way because shoppers see the left digit first.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Sales tax: In the United States sales tax varies by state and even city, while in much of the world VAT is already included in prices.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Store name: The store logo at the top helps with returns, and receipts are an old way to prove where a thing was bought.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Change given: Cashiers once counted change upward from the price to the amount handed over, a method called counting up.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Item names: The item list uses abbreviated names, because early receipt printers had limited characters per line.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Time: The printed time helps shops check cameras and staff schedules, and it can settle disputes about when you bought something.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Subtotal: The subtotal is the sum before tax, and it matters when discounts or taxes are applied afterward.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Barcode: The first product scanned with a barcode was a pack of Wrigley's gum in 1974, in Ohio.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Cashier name: A cashier's name or ID on the receipt makes it easier to resolve errors, and some shops add it for tipping.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Return policy: The return policy is usually in small print at the bottom, and it often lists the number of days you have.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Weather forecast: A trap: a receipt prints what you bought, not the future, though some apps could pair one with a forecast.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Horoscope: Newspapers print horoscopes, though a receipt would only tell your total.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Recipe: Cookbooks hold recipes, whereas receipts are only evidence of a purchase, though 'receipt' meant a recipe in old English.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Blood type: Blood type is medical, and a shop has no reason to know it.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Crossword: Crosswords appear on newspaper pages, and the first printed one was by Arthur Wynne in 1913.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Map: A store map is posted in-store, and receipts rarely include one.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Sports scores: Scores belong on a scoreboard or a news site, and a receipt is just a list of what you bought.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Your PIN: PINs never print on a receipt, and card numbers are masked with stars for the same reason.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Cat photo: Cat photos are plentiful online, but receipts tend to be plain thermal paper in black and white.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Shoe size: Shoe size would only be on the box label for a shoe, not on a receipt.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Password: A password on a receipt would be a security risk, which is why shops never print one.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Movie review: A reviewer's opinion lives in a newspaper, and a receipt just says what you paid.
Things printed on a shop receipt.Bedtime story: The thermal paper is too thin for a story, though fiction written on receipts is a real art project.

Things that make you sneeze.Pollen: Allergic immune systems mistake harmless pollen for a threat and release histamine, which is what antihistamine pills block.
Things that make you sneeze.Dust: Dust is full of skin flakes, fibers and tiny particles that tickle the nose lining and set off a sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Black pepper: Piperine in black pepper irritates nasal nerve endings, which is why a whiff sets off a sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Cat dander: The allergen is mainly a protein called Fel d 1 in skin flakes and saliva, not the hair itself.
Things that make you sneeze.Ragweed: Ragweed is a leading cause of autumn hay fever in North America, and a single plant can release a billion grains of pollen.
Things that make you sneeze.Mold spores: Mold spores float in damp air, indoors and out, and breathing them in can trigger sneezing and allergies.
Things that make you sneeze.Hay fever: Despite its name, hay fever involves no hay and no fever; it's an allergic reaction to airborne pollen.
Things that make you sneeze.Dust mites: These microscopic relatives of spiders live in bedding, and it's their droppings that people react to.
Things that make you sneeze.Common cold: A cold virus makes the nose lining inflamed, and sneezing sprays droplets that can travel several meters.
Things that make you sneeze.Feather in the nose: A tickle in the nose is a classic trigger, since the nasal nerves can't tell a feather from an irritant.
Things that make you sneeze.Chopping onions: A trap: onions make you cry, not sneeze. Cutting them releases a gas that stings your eyes.
Things that make you sneeze.Drinking water: Water doesn't trigger sneezes, though if it goes down the wrong way it will make you cough instead.
Things that make you sneeze.Seeing someone yawn: Yawns are contagious, but they make you yawn and not sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Gulping ice cream: Gulping ice cream causes a brain freeze headache from a cold palate, not a sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Spinning around: Spinning causes dizziness through your inner ear and has no direct link to sneezing.
Things that make you sneeze.Eating beans: Beans may cause gas, but they won't make you sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Scary movies: Fear raises your heart rate and adrenaline, but it doesn't set off a sneeze.
Things that make you sneeze.Loud music: Loud noise can damage hearing but doesn't trigger sneezing.
Things that make you sneeze.Sad movies: Sadness makes you cry, and while tears drain through the nose, that doesn't cause sneezing.
Things that make you sneeze.Warm milk: Warm milk is a comforting bedtime drink with no connection to sneezes.
Things that make you sneeze.Getting tickled: Tickling provokes laughter and squirming, not sneezing, though a tickle inside the nose does.
Things that make you sneeze.Bananas: Bananas won't make you sneeze, though they do give some people with latex allergy a reaction.
Things that make you sneeze.Long car rides: Long car rides cause motion sickness for some, not sneezing.
Things that make you sneeze.Hot bath: A hot bath relaxes you and doesn't cause sneezing, though steam can ease a stuffy nose.

Things people take for a cold.Chicken soup: Studies suggest chicken soup may mildly slow inflammatory white cells, and the steam helps clear the nose too.
Things people take for a cold.Honey: Honey is a proven cough soother and, according to research, works about as well as some cough medicines, but is unsafe for infants under one.
Things people take for a cold.Hot tea: Warm tea soothes a sore throat and hydrates you, though a cold virus itself isn't cured by it.
Things people take for a cold.Lemon: Lemon juice supplies vitamin C, though research shows it won't prevent or cure a cold by itself.
Things people take for a cold.Ginger: Ginger has been used for sore throats and nausea for thousands of years in Chinese and Indian medicine.
Things people take for a cold.Throat lozenge: Lozenges make you produce more saliva, which coats and soothes an irritated throat.
Things people take for a cold.Steam: Warm steam loosens mucus and eases a stuffy nose, though it won't shorten the cold.
Things people take for a cold.Vapor rub: Menthol in vapor rub tricks cold receptors into feeling like easier breathing, yet it doesn't actually open airways.
Things people take for a cold.Rest: Sleep boosts your immune system, and sleeping enough can help your body clear a cold faster.
Things people take for a cold.Orange juice: Orange juice is a classic cold remedy, yet vitamin C doesn't prevent colds in most people.
Things people take for a cold.Garlic: Garlic has compounds like allicin with some antimicrobial action, but evidence for treating a cold is thin.
Things people take for a cold.Cough syrup: Cough syrups often contain dextromethorphan, a cough suppressant that works on the brain's cough reflex.
Things people take for a cold.Saline spray: Saltwater spray thins mucus and rinses the nose gently, and it's safe for babies as well.
Things people take for a cold.Cotton candy: A trap: cotton candy is spun sugar, and it was invented by a dentist in 1897, so it won't help a cold.
Things people take for a cold.Energy drink: Energy drinks mask tiredness with caffeine, but a sick body needs real rest and fluids.
Things people take for a cold.Cold pizza: The chilled leftover may be beloved for breakfast, but it does nothing for a cold.
Things people take for a cold.Bubble gum: Bubble gum gets its pink color from a 1928 formula, and it offers no cold relief.
Things people take for a cold.Jumping jacks: Hard exercise is better skipped with a fever, though light movement is fine with only a head cold.
Things people take for a cold.Fried chicken: Fried chicken is not the same as chicken soup, and its grease won't soothe a cold.
Things people take for a cold.Cola: Soda's sugar and fizz can irritate a sore throat, and flat cola is a belly-ache folk remedy instead.
Things people take for a cold.Potato chips: Potato chips were allegedly born from a customer complaining about thick fries in 1853, and they do nothing for a cold.
Things people take for a cold.Cheesecake: Cheesecake is a dessert, and the ancient Greeks may have served it to Olympic athletes.
Things people take for a cold.Popcorn: Popcorn is whole-grain corn that pops when its moisture turns to steam, but it doesn't treat colds.
Things people take for a cold.Hot dog: Hot dogs got their name from the sausages' dachshund shape, and they won't treat a cold.

Animals that could outrun you.Cheetah: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100 kilometers per hour, but only for short sprints of several hundred meters.
Animals that could outrun you.Horse: A galloping horse reaches about 55 kilometers per hour, and the fastest human sprinters top out around 37.
Animals that could outrun you.Greyhound: A greyhound can run about 70 kilometers per hour, which makes the breed the fastest dog, and far faster than any person.
Animals that could outrun you.Ostrich: An ostrich can run about 70 kilometers per hour and keep up a quick pace for a long time, the fastest bird on land.
Animals that could outrun you.Kangaroo: A red kangaroo can hop at over 50 kilometers per hour, and its tendons store energy like a spring.
Animals that could outrun you.Deer: Many deer can run around 50 kilometers per hour, far faster than any person, and can leap fences.
Animals that could outrun you.House cat: A house cat can sprint about 48 kilometers per hour, which is faster than Usain Bolt at his peak.
Animals that could outrun you.Elephant: An elephant can move at about 25 kilometers per hour when it charges, which is faster than most people can sprint.
Animals that could outrun you.Hippo: A hippo, surprisingly, can run about 30 kilometers per hour over short distances, and it is dangerous.
Animals that could outrun you.Grizzly bear: A grizzly can run about 55 kilometers per hour, even uphill, so never try to outrun one, since you will lose.
Animals that could outrun you.Giraffe: A giraffe can run about 60 kilometers per hour, and its long legs cover about four meters a stride.
Animals that could outrun you.Zebra: A zebra can run about 65 kilometers per hour, and its stripes may help confuse biting flies.
Animals that could outrun you.Tortoise: A tortoise moves at around 0.3 kilometers per hour, though it can live well over a century.
Animals that could outrun you.Sloth: A sloth moves about a few meters a minute, and it descends from its tree about once a week.
Animals that could outrun you.Snail: A garden snail moves about a meter in 20 minutes, so almost anything, and certainly any walking human, can beat it.
Animals that could outrun you.Penguin: A penguin waddles at only about 3 kilometers per hour on land, though in water it is a fast swimmer.
Animals that could outrun you.Turtle: A sea turtle is a graceful swimmer, but on land it crawls slowly, at about 1 kilometer per hour at most.
Animals that could outrun you.Hedgehog: A hedgehog can scurry about 6 kilometers per hour, so a person can outrun it easily, and when afraid it rolls into a ball.
Animals that could outrun you.Hamster: A hamster can run a lot on its wheel, up to several kilometers a night, but it is not fast.
Animals that could outrun you.Slug: A slug travels only about 15 centimeters a minute, leaving a mucus trail that helps it glide.
Animals that could outrun you.Starfish: A starfish creeps along on hundreds of tiny tube feet, at a speed of a few centimeters a minute.
Animals that could outrun you.Earthworm: An earthworm crawls at a few centimeters a minute, a pace far slower than any human walk, so you can easily outrun one.
Animals that could outrun you.Ladybug: A ladybug flies surprisingly well, but on the ground it only crawls slowly, and a person easily outpaces one.
Animals that could outrun you.Caterpillar: A caterpillar crawls only a few centimeters a second at best, while it eats leaves nonstop and grows many times its size.

Things in a courtroom.Judge: In common-law courts the judge acts as referee over the rules and in jury trials leaves the verdict to twelve ordinary citizens.
Things in a courtroom.Gavel: The gavel is far more common in movies than in real life, and many judges quietly never use one.
Things in a courtroom.Jury box: Twelve is a traditional jury size in many common-law countries, a custom that goes back centuries in England.
Things in a courtroom.Witness stand: Witnesses swear or affirm to tell the truth here, and lying under oath is the crime of perjury.
Things in a courtroom.Bailiff: The bailiff keeps order, escorts the jury and calls the room to rise when the judge enters.
Things in a courtroom.Bench: The judge's raised bench is a visual cue of authority; the word is also used to mean the judges collectively, as in "on the bench."
Things in a courtroom.Court reporter: Using a stenotype machine, a good reporter can record over 200 words a minute, producing the official transcript.
Things in a courtroom.Defendant: The accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and in many systems the burden of proof rests entirely on the other side.
Things in a courtroom.Prosecutor: In many countries the prosecutor represents the state, and a key job is deciding whether there's enough evidence to bring a case.
Things in a courtroom.Defense attorney: Even a client who has confessed is entitled to a lawyer, because the right to counsel is a pillar of a fair trial.
Things in a courtroom.Public gallery: Open trials are a safeguard against secret justice, so ordinary citizens and journalists are generally free to watch.
Things in a courtroom.Referee: Refs oversee games, not trials; they're the sports counterpart to a judge but keep time with a whistle, not a gavel.
Things in a courtroom.Umpire: Baseball and cricket use umpires, who make calls on the field, so it's a sports official rather than a court one.
Things in a courtroom.Scoreboard: Courts don't keep a score; a verdict is either guilty or not guilty, not decided on points.
Things in a courtroom.Altar: An altar is for worship, and the oath taken in court, though once often sworn on a holy book, is now commonly secular.
Things in a courtroom.Chef: Chefs cook in a kitchen, not a courtroom, though a trial may call a chef as a witness in a poisoning or food-safety case.
Things in a courtroom.Scalpel: A surgeon's blade belongs in an operating room, though forensic experts may appear in court to explain what one did.
Things in a courtroom.Easel: Easels hold paintings, but court artists sketch trials where cameras aren't allowed, often on pads in their laps.
Things in a courtroom.Cash register: This is for a shop; a court's fines are paid at a clerk's window, not at a till.
Things in a courtroom.Treadmill: A treadmill is a gym machine, but it was originally a 19th-century prison punishment, so it does have a legal history.
Things in a courtroom.Jukebox: A jukebox plays songs in a bar; the only music in a courtroom is none at all.
Things in a courtroom.Bunsen burner: This lab flame belongs to science classes, though forensic labs may use one to supply the evidence heard in court.
Things in a courtroom.Surfboard: Surfboards belong on the beach, and the only wave in court is the one a judge makes to quiet the room.
Things in a courtroom.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a farm tool, and the image of angry mobs with pitchforks is what a fair trial is meant to replace.

Jobs ending in '-ist'.Dentist: The first dental school, in Baltimore in 1840, helped turn dentistry into a profession and not a side job of barbers.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Pharmacist: Pharmacist comes from the Greek 'pharmakon', meaning drug, and it ends in -ist, so it fits the pattern.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Florist: The biggest days of the year for US florists are usually Valentine's Day and Mother's Day.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Chemist: Chemist ends in -ist, so it fits. In Britain, 'chemist' is also the everyday word for a pharmacy.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Cartoonist: A cartoonist draws comics or satirical sketches, and the word comes from the large paper sketches called cartoons.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Novelist: A novelist writes long fiction, and the word comes from the Italian 'novella', meaning 'new'.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Journalist: A journalist reports the news, and the word comes from French 'journal', meaning daily, so it ends in -ist and fits.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Therapist: Therapist comes from the Greek 'therapeia', meaning healing, and ends in -ist, so it fits the pattern.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Pianist: A pianist plays the piano. The name 'piano' is short for pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because it can vary volume.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Biologist: The word 'biology' was coined around 1800, apparently independently by Lamarck and Treviranus.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Economist: An economist studies how people use scarce resources. Adam Smith, author of The Wealth of Nations, is often called the father of economics.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Typist: Typists were in great demand after the typewriter became practical in the 1870s and 1880s.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Electrician: Electrician ends in -ian, not -ist, and so it's a trap, even though the job is very familiar.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Musician: Musician ends in -ian, not -ist, so it doesn't fit. Pianists are musicians, but 'pianist' does fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Physician: Physician ends in -ian, not -ist. Despite the similar ending to 'dentist', it doesn't fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Magician: Magician ends in -ian, not -ist, even though it sounds like it ought to match the list of jobs.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Surgeon: A surgeon ends in -eon, a word from the Greek 'cheirourgos', or hand-worker, so it doesn't fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Plumber: A plumber ends in -er, and the word comes from the Latin 'plumbum' for lead, which was used for pipes.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Lawyer: A lawyer ends in -er, so it doesn't fit the -ist pattern, even though lawyers are specialists.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Pilot: A pilot ends in -ot, and the word comes from Italian roots for a steersman, so it doesn't fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Barber: A barber comes from the Latin 'barba', for beard, and ends in -er, so it doesn't fit the pattern.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Architect: An architect ends in -ect. It comes from the Greek 'arkhitekton', meaning chief builder, so it doesn't fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Optician: An optician ends in -ian. It's easily confused with the optometrist, but still doesn't fit.
Jobs ending in '-ist'.Librarian: A librarian ends in -ian, not -ist. It follows the same pattern as musician and magician instead.

Electronic toys.Furby: Its 1998 craze spoke Furbish and slowly picked up English; the NSA reportedly banned it from its offices over recording fears.
Electronic toys.Tamagotchi: Japan's 1996 virtual pet let neglected creatures 'die' and went on to sell over 80 million units worldwide.
Electronic toys.Speak & Spell: This 1978 talking spelling toy from Texas Instruments was used in E.T. to phone home.
Electronic toys.Tickle Me Elmo: Its 1996 holiday shortage turned shoppers into brawlers at store doors across America.
Electronic toys.Bop It: Hasbro's 1996 game shouts commands such as 'Twist it!' and speeds up as you succeed.
Electronic toys.Simon: Co-created by Ralph Baer, the inventor of the first home video game console, in 1978.
Electronic toys.Teddy Ruxpin: Its 1985 stories ran on cassette tapes, where one track carried the audio and another moved its mouth and eyes.
Electronic toys.Hatchimals: The 2016 egg-shaped creatures needed a hatching process, and sold out at holiday time.
Electronic toys.Zhu Zhu Pets: The 2009 robot hamsters cost about ten dollars and were a holiday hit, sold out for weeks.
Electronic toys.Robosapien: Designed by robotics physicist Mark Tilden using simple analog circuits, it sold over a million units in the 2000s.
Electronic toys.Remote-control car: Hobby-grade versions today can top 100 miles per hour.
Electronic toys.Etch A Sketch: A purely mechanical sketch toy: aluminum powder behind the screen is scraped away by a stylus; invented by Frenchman André Cassagnes.
Electronic toys.Rubik's Cube: Fully mechanical, with about 43 quintillion possible arrangements.
Electronic toys.Slinky: Invented by accident in 1943 when engineer Richard James saw a torsion spring fall off a shelf; no batteries needed.
Electronic toys.Lego: The name comes from the Danish 'leg godt', meaning play well.
Electronic toys.Yo-yo: Ancient Greek vase paintings from around 500 BC show yo-yos, but they're spring-free and battery-free.
Electronic toys.Play-Doh: Started life as a wallpaper cleaner before becoming a modeling clay for kids.
Electronic toys.Hula hoop: Wham-O's 1958 craze, with millions sold within months, needed nothing but a swinging waist.
Electronic toys.Magic 8 Ball: Inside is a 20-sided die floating in blue liquid, with ten positive, five neutral and five negative answers.
Electronic toys.Frisbee: Inspired by pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company, which students tossed around.
Electronic toys.Silly Putty: Discovered accidentally during World War II while researching synthetic rubber.
Electronic toys.Mr. Potato Head: In 1952, the first toy advertised on TV, and it was originally sold as pieces to stick into a real potato.
Electronic toys.Jenga: Created by Leslie Scott; the name comes from the Swahili 'kujenga', meaning to build.
Electronic toys.Spirograph: The gear-based drawing toy was invented by Denys Fisher in the 1960s and needs only pens and paper.

Works by Michelangelo.David: Carved from a marble block other sculptors had abandoned, finished in 1504, and nearly 17 feet tall.
Works by Michelangelo.Sistine Chapel: He painted the ceiling for Pope Julius II from 1508 to 1512, working mostly standing, not lying on his back as legend has it.
Works by Michelangelo.Pietà: His only signed work, with his name carved on the sash across Mary's chest, in St Peter's Basilica.
Works by Michelangelo.Creation of Adam: Its nearly touching fingers are the most copied detail of the Sistine ceiling; God's finger is the one reaching toward Adam.
Works by Michelangelo.The Last Judgment: Painted on the Sistine Chapel's altar wall; the flayed skin held by St Bartholomew is said to carry Michelangelo's own face.
Works by Michelangelo.Moses: Made for Pope Julius II's tomb; the horns on his head come from a mistranslation of the Hebrew Bible.
Works by Michelangelo.Doni Tondo: A round painting of the Holy Family, one of the few panel paintings firmly attributed to him.
Works by Michelangelo.Bacchus: An early marble from 1496-97 of the wine god, shown tipsily swaying; it made his name in Rome.
Works by Michelangelo.Dying Slave: One of two slave statues made for Julius II's tomb, with a figure that seems to be sinking into rest; now in the Louvre.
Works by Michelangelo.Mona Lisa: Leonardo's painting, not Michelangelo's; the two rivals worked in Florence in the same years.
Works by Michelangelo.The Last Supper: Leonardo's wall painting in Milan; its experimental technique began flaking within decades.
Works by Michelangelo.The Birth of Venus: Botticelli's painting, with Venus on a shell, hangs in the Uffizi in Florence and is not by Michelangelo.
Works by Michelangelo.The Thinker: Rodin's bronze, not Michelangelo's; it began as the figure of Dante in The Gates of Hell.
Works by Michelangelo.Venus de Milo: A marble Greek statue found on Milos in 1820, famous for its missing arms; far older than Michelangelo.
Works by Michelangelo.The Kiss: Klimt painted a golden one in 1907-08; Rodin also sculpted one, but neither is Michelangelo.
Works by Michelangelo.The School of Athens: Raphael's fresco in the Vatican; he is said to have given Michelangelo's face to Heraclitus.
Works by Michelangelo.Primavera: Botticelli's painting full of spring figures and flowers, not Michelangelo's; it shares the Uffizi with Birth of Venus.
Works by Michelangelo.The Night Watch: Rembrandt's 1642 group portrait of a militia company, in Amsterdam; its name comes from darkened varnish.
Works by Michelangelo.Discobolus: A Greek discus thrower by Myron, known mainly through Roman copies, not Michelangelo's.
Works by Michelangelo.Apollo and Daphne: Bernini's Baroque marble, from the 1620s, shows Daphne turning into a tree; it is not Michelangelo's.
Works by Michelangelo.Winged Victory: A Hellenistic Greek statue in the Louvre, headless but dramatic, made centuries before Michelangelo was born.
Works by Michelangelo.Statue of Liberty: Bartholdi's copper statue of 1886 has an iron frame designed by Gustave Eiffel's engineering.
Works by Michelangelo.Water Lilies: Monet painted around 250 of these in his Giverny garden, long after Michelangelo's lifetime.
Works by Michelangelo.Guernica: Picasso's 1937 black-and-white response to the bombing of a Basque town, in a modern style far from Michelangelo.

Musicals based on books.Les Misérables: Victor Hugo's 1862 novel became a musical that premiered in Paris in 1980 and in London in 1985, now one of the longest-running shows.
Musicals based on books.Wicked: Gregory Maguire's 1995 novel retells The Wizard of Oz from the Wicked Witch's side; the musical opened in 2003.
Musicals based on books.Oliver!: Lionel Bart's 1960 show is based on Dickens's Oliver Twist; the 1968 film version won the Best Picture Oscar.
Musicals based on books.Matilda: Roald Dahl's 1988 novel became a 2010 musical with songs by comedian Tim Minchin, first staged by the Royal Shakespeare Company.
Musicals based on books.Phantom of the Opera: Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel inspired Andrew Lloyd Webber's show, which ran on Broadway for 35 years until 2023.
Musicals based on books.Cats: It's based on T. S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats (1939), poems he originally wrote for his godchildren.
Musicals based on books.Hamilton: Lin-Manuel Miranda read Ron Chernow's 2004 biography of Alexander Hamilton on vacation and turned it into a hip-hop musical.
Musicals based on books.Mary Poppins: P. L. Travers wrote the books starting in 1934, and reportedly disliked Disney's film adaptation.
Musicals based on books.Little Women: Louisa May Alcott's 1868 novel about four March sisters was turned into a Broadway musical in 2005.
Musicals based on books.Man of La Mancha: Based on Cervantes's Don Quixote, it gave the world the song "The Impossible Dream".
Musicals based on books.The Secret Garden: Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 novel became a 1991 musical, and Daisy Eagan won a Tony at age 11 for it.
Musicals based on books.Big Fish: Daniel Wallace's 1998 novel about a father's tall tales became a Tim Burton film in 2003, then a musical.
Musicals based on books.Grease: Grease was written for the stage in Chicago in 1971 from the creators' own memories, rather than from a book.
Musicals based on books.Six: Six is an original pop-concert musical about Henry VIII's wives, written by two Cambridge students.
Musicals based on books.Hairspray: Hairspray was adapted from John Waters's 1988 film, not a book.
Musicals based on books.Mamma Mia!: Mamma Mia! weaves together ABBA's songs into a new story, written for the stage.
Musicals based on books.The Producers: The Producers is adapted from Mel Brooks's 1967 film, not a novel.
Musicals based on books.Spamalot: Spamalot is lovingly ripped off from the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, not a book.
Musicals based on books.Dreamgirls: Dreamgirls was inspired by the story of the Supremes and Motown, not a novel.
Musicals based on books.A Chorus Line: A Chorus Line grew from recorded interviews with Broadway dancers, not a book.
Musicals based on books.Jersey Boys: Jersey Boys tells the real story of the Four Seasons, using their hit songs.
Musicals based on books.Come From Away: Come From Away dramatizes the real welcome Gander, Newfoundland gave to stranded flights after 9/11.
Musicals based on books.Kinky Boots: Kinky Boots was adapted from a 2005 British film, itself based on a true story of a shoe factory.
Musicals based on books.Sister Act: Sister Act came from the 1992 film starring Whoopi Goldberg, not a book.

Novels titled after their main character.Ivanhoe: Walter Scott's 1819 novel gave us the modern image of Robin Hood, here as Locksley.
Novels titled after their main character.Madame Bovary: Flaubert was put on trial for obscenity over Madame Bovary in 1857 and acquitted; the heroine is Emma Bovary.
Novels titled after their main character.Anna Karenina: Tolstoy opens it with 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.'
Novels titled after their main character.Robinson Crusoe: Defoe's 1719 novel was partly inspired by the real castaway Alexander Selkirk.
Novels titled after their main character.Don Quixote: Cervantes's book gave English the word 'quixotic', and is often called the first modern novel.
Novels titled after their main character.Siddhartha: Hermann Hesse's hero shares a name with the Buddha, but is another man of the same period.
Novels titled after their main character.Persuasion: Austen's last completed novel is named for an abstract idea, not for its heroine Anne Elliot.
Novels titled after their main character.Middlemarch: Named for a fictional English town; George Eliot's novel follows several people, with Dorothea Brooke the most prominent.
Novels titled after their main character.Ulysses: Joyce's novel takes the Latin form of Odysseus, but the hero is Leopold Bloom, so it doesn't fit.
Novels titled after their main character.Wuthering Heights: The title names a windswept Yorkshire farmhouse; Emily Brontë's only novel centers on Heathcliff and Catherine.
Novels titled after their main character.Great Expectations: The title refers to what Pip hopes for, not Pip himself, and Dickens first published it in weekly installments.
Novels titled after their main character.Bleak House: Named for a house, in a novel about the endless Chancery lawsuit Jarndyce and Jarndyce, not for a person.
Novels titled after their main character.Little Women: Named for the four March sisters as a group, not one main character, so it doesn't fit.
Novels titled after their main character.Dune: Dune is named for a desert planet's landscape, Arrakis, and not for its hero Paul Atreides.
Novels titled after their main character.Holes: The title refers to what the boys dig; the hero is Stanley Yelnats, whose name is a palindrome.
Novels titled after their main character.Atonement: McEwan's title names a theme, Briony's guilt, rather than a character, so it doesn't fit.
Novels titled after their main character.Germinal: Germinal is a month of the French Revolutionary calendar, 'time of germination', and Zola's miners' novel is named for it, not a person.
